homeschoolingwithpurpose.excerpt:
Scripture reading · James 1:2-8, 19

What are we trying to change?

By Thursday night, Nora's mother, Ruth, had priced two complete curricula. Nora had come home discouraged after another reading assignment, and Ruth wanted to give her a fresh start. When Ruth asked what she would change about her school day, Nora said, “I want help remembering what happened in the story. I want to keep seeing my friends.” Ruth closed the shopping tabs. There were now two things for the family to protect, and neither appeared on the curriculum checklist.

James begins his letter by addressing believers facing trials. He describes how the testing of faith can produce patience, then invites anyone who lacks wisdom to ask God, who gives generously. Asking in faith means coming to God with confidence in His generosity. The passage gives a family reason to pray honestly amid uncertainty and to give patience time to work. Later in the chapter, James calls believers to be quick to hear and slow to speak. Ruth can act on that counsel by letting Nora finish a thought before asking her next question.

Ask each person what they would keep, what they would change, and what they can contribute. Children can often describe a difficult moment more clearly than they can explain its cause. Invite your child to show you a recent example. Ask, “Where did this start to feel hard?” Then try one small support and observe what happens. Record the child's words alongside your own observation. A child who reads aloud easily and struggles to organize a retelling may need a different first lesson from a child who has difficulty reading the words on the page.

With a short story about a lost dog, Nora read the words aloud and remembered how the dog got home. When Ruth asked how the search began, Nora jumped from the ending to the middle. Three index cards gave her somewhere to put the events while she thought. That one observation gave the family a skill to work on and a question to bring to the teacher.

Decide what you can carry

Ruth and Daniel, Nora's father, compared two options against the same goal. Nora would use three picture cards to tell the main events of an unfamiliar short story in order. Her teacher offered to provide one short passage a week and suggest a way to prompt a retelling. Staying enrolled during a four-week trial preserved Nora's friendships and allowed the family to try targeted support. Learning at home could give Nora more flexibility and let her work on reading while she was fresh. It would also require an adult to take responsibility for the rest of the learning day, a plan for her younger brother Eli, and predictable contact with friends.

Daniel could teach on Tuesday and Thursday before leaving for work, but the family's first idea depended on Ruth having every weekday morning free. She worked two early shifts. They drew a real week on paper and agreed to try teacher-supported practice first. Ruth took a short Monday session, Daniel took Thursday, and Saturday was available only if Nora wanted to make up a missed practice. They asked the teacher what to look for and chose a date for reviewing the evidence together. A week with an unexpected shift change still had one dependable session.

Family exercise. Make two columns for workable options. Under each, write how the child will practice, who will teach, how the child will stay connected to friends, what it will cost, and what evidence you will review. Circle any promise that depends on unconfirmed help. Give the child a private way to share a concern before the decision is made.

Pray together. “Father, thank You for giving wisdom generously. Help us listen with patience, see what our child needs, and follow through on the responsibilities we accept. Give our child courage to tell us what is hard and what is helping. Amen.”

Listen before you decide

Nora answered the first question with a concern about her friends. Ruth wanted to hear an answer about reading. By writing down what Nora actually said, she kept an important part of the decision from disappearing. The two concerns belonged on the same page because either option would affect both.

Start with a moment the child can remember. Ask them to walk you through it from the beginning. Where were they sitting? What were they asked to do? When did they lose track? Let them show you a piece of work, draw the setting, or speak while you take a short walk. A child who has heard a great deal of adult discussion may need time to form an answer of their own.

Reflect back one sentence and ask if you have it right. Ruth said, “It sounds as if you can read the story but lose your place when someone asks about everything that happened.” Nora corrected her. “I remember the end. I don't remember what I should say first.” That distinction helped Ruth prepare one small task instead of correcting every part of Nora's retelling.

Use the same care with the adults. If a parent says a morning is free, check whether they mean every morning or one particular morning. Ask about the part of the work that is hardest to picture. A family can agree in principle and still need different amounts of preparation, rest, or help before it can carry the plan.

Write three notes after the conversation: the child's own words, one detail an adult learned, and one question the family will investigate. Read them back together so each person can correct the record.

servantleadershipforministryteams.section: Chapter 1 · Communicate so people can act
servantleadershipforministryteams.excerpt:
Scripture reading · James 1:19-25 and Ephesians 4:11-16

Listen for what the volunteer actually heard

At Hope Street Church, the Sunday school team agreed that a new family should hear from someone before the next class. On Thursday the coordinator, Miriam, learned that no one had called. Naomi had heard a request to send an email. Gabriel thought Miriam was making the call. The parent had asked for a phone call after work. Everyone had wanted to help, yet the family still had to wait.

James tells believers to be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger. He goes on to call them to receive the word and do what it says. A leader can obey that instruction in a meeting by resisting the impulse to explain away a problem and hearing the volunteer's account before assigning blame. Ephesians 4 places speaking the truth in love within a larger picture of the body growing up into Christ. Christ gives people to equip His people for ministry, and the body grows as its members do their work together. Truth and love shape the way a leader makes the work clear and receives an honest answer about it.

Ask what the volunteer understood and what could keep them from doing it. A volunteer may be able to make a call after work but need an approved way to reach the parent. Another may only have time to prepare the class information. Those two contributions can work together if the team agrees where one ends and the other begins. A leader who listens early has time to make a realistic assignment.

At the next meeting Miriam brought up the missed call without identifying the family to people who did not need the details. She asked Naomi and Gabriel to describe their understanding. She also named her part in the confusion. “I asked us to follow up and never confirmed who would do it.” That sentence made it easier for Naomi to say she could make the call if the task and the contact details were shared through the church's usual process.

Agree on a next step and a time to check it

Miriam confirmed the parent's request, then asked Naomi to call by Wednesday evening and offer the Sunday school time and entrance information. Naomi would tell Miriam by Thursday whether they had connected. If the family asked to stop receiving calls, she would record that preference through the team's approved process. Miriam gave Naomi only the information needed for the call.

Naomi repeated what she understood. She had heard “call every evening until you reach the parent.” Miriam meant one attempt followed by a check-in. They corrected that detail while they were still together. Miriam recorded the action, owner, deadline, and check-in. Gabriel prepared the Sunday school directions for Naomi to use. The team could now tell what each person had agreed to and when to look for a result.

If an assignment goes wrong, speak privately with the person involved and describe what you observed. Ask what happened and hear the answer. If someone needs to step back, agree on who will take over and how the original assignment will be closed. Two people calling with the same message can confuse a family that asked for one contact.

Team exercise. Bring one task your team lost track of twice. Identify whether the gap was the assignment, the resources, the deadline, or the check-in. Write a four-line handoff with the person being served, the promised action, the owner and deadline, and the time you will review it. Ask the owner to say it back in their own words.

Pray together. “Father, teach us to hear one another fully and to speak with truth and love. Help us keep the promises people are waiting on. Amen.”

Find the point where the message changed

A missed assignment gives you something to investigate. Begin with the actual instruction and the moment it was given. Ask each person what they thought would happen next. If two people heard different things, find the words that let both readings make sense. An instruction such as “let's follow up” can sound like agreement on a purpose even while leaving the action unassigned.

At Hope Street, Gabriel knew the service time and could prepare the directions. Naomi could make the call after work. Miriam had the parent's permission and access to the contact detail. The useful instruction had to connect three contributions. The team could divide the task cleanly once it could describe where each person's work ended.

Exercise. Ask two people to repeat a recent team instruction in their own words. Write down where their answers differ. Identify whether the uncertainty is about the action, the deadline, access, or who has responsibility. Rewrite the instruction and ask the person carrying it what is still unclear.

praywithconfidence.excerpt:
Scripture reading · Philippians 4:2-9

Give the need a name

Paul's words about prayer come near the close of a letter to believers he loves. He urges two women in the church to agree in the Lord, calls the church to gentleness, and reminds them that the Lord is near. He invites them to make their requests known to God by prayer and petition with thanksgiving. The peace of God guards their hearts and minds in Christ. Paul then directs their attention to what is true and worthy of praise and to the practice of what they have learned.

Naming a request clearly helps us bring the actual burden before God. It can also show what responsibility is already ours. A prayer about tomorrow may contain a fear about disappointing someone, a need for daily provision, and a conversation that has been delayed. Give those concerns words. Thanksgiving can name help already received while the main question remains open.

Grace had been praying, “Lord, fix this week.” When she sat down with her schedule, she realized she needed two work commitments clarified before she could promise to help her sister move. She prayed for a fair and clear conversation, thanked God for a colleague who had previously covered a shift, and wrote down the question she would ask her supervisor. She told her sister when she could give a dependable answer. Over the next two days she prayed again as she waited for a reply.

Exercise. Write three sentences. “Here is what I am asking You for.” “Here is a mercy I can thank You for today.” “Here is one responsibility I can carry.” Read them as a prayer and put the action on your calendar. When the matter comes to mind again, give God a fresh sentence about the concern and return to the next responsibility in front of you.

Reflection. What would make this request clearer? Is there a promise, conversation, or small act of preparation you can address while you wait?

Separate the concern from the request

A concern often arrives as a mixture of events, feelings, and unfinished decisions. A request tells God what you are asking for in that situation. Give yourself permission to describe both. “I am worried about the call” may lead to “Please give me courage to ask the question plainly and listen to the answer.”

Grace needed to know which shifts she could commit to before helping her sister move. She wrote the known dates on a page and separated them from her fear that both people would be disappointed. She could pray honestly about the fear and ask for an answer about the schedule. That gave her a useful question to bring to her supervisor.

Exercise. Write two sentences about the facts you know, one about what you feel, and one clear request. Read the four lines as a prayer. If the situation contains several decisions, start with the one you can identify and return to the others later.

Give thanks for a mercy you can name

In Philippians 4, thanksgiving accompanies prayer and petition. A specific mercy can be remembered while an urgent request is still open. Recall a person who kept a promise, a word of encouragement, or help you had overlooked. Thank God for what you actually received.

Grace thanked God for the colleague who had covered a previous shift. That memory reminded her that she could ask about available options. It also gave her a reason to thank the colleague without asking for another favor. The gratitude was genuine even while the new schedule remained undecided.

Exercise. Put a line for thanks beside one request in your notebook. Include the detail that makes the mercy recognizable: the time, the person, or the action. Pray both lines. Later, see whether the note gives you a clearer account of what helped that week.

forgivingwithwisdom.section: Chapter 1 · Tell the truth about the hurt
forgivingwithwisdom.excerpt:
Scripture reading · Psalm 13

Bring the whole sentence to God

Psalm 13 begins with repeated questions about how long suffering will last. The psalmist describes sorrow and asks the Lord to look and answer. He ends by trusting God's steadfast love and looking toward praise. The complaint has a place in the same prayer as trust. A reader can bring God a particular wound and ask for help before they can see what the whole story will become.

Martha had told her cousin Lydia about a financial difficulty and asked her to keep it private. At a family meal another relative referred to it. Martha laughed and changed the subject. At home she told herself she was making too much of it. When she began writing privately, she was able to describe the event in three sentences. “I asked Lydia to keep the conversation private. Another relative knew enough to mention it in front of the family. I felt exposed and have been avoiding the family chat.” Those sentences gave her something specific to bring before God.

Separate what you know from what you are still trying to understand. Martha knew that her private information had reached a wider audience. She did not yet know how many people had heard it or why Lydia had told someone. Writing both categories helped her avoid guessing at motives and gave her language to talk with a trusted person if she chose to. The first step was truthfulness in God's presence. She kept the account in a private place.

Exercise. Write what happened in a sentence that names the action. Write its effect in a second sentence and what you need today in a third. Add one unresolved question if there is one. You may pray over the page privately or share as much as you choose with someone you trust.

Pray together. “Father, You see what happened and what it cost me. Give me courage to bring You the truth and grace to hear what I need for the next step. Amen.”

Write the event in terms you can stand behind

Start with what you saw, heard, or were told. Include the setting and the action that mattered. If you heard about something secondhand, keep that distinction. A clear account gives you words to use in prayer and a way to decide whether you need to ask a question.

Martha knew someone at dinner had repeated private information. She could quote the words she remembered and describe the agreement she had made with Lydia. She could only guess how many people knew. Her first note kept those facts separate. It helped her bring an honest account to God without repeating a rumor about what Lydia intended.

Exercise. Write one sentence for what you know and one for what remains unclear. Record only what is necessary. If writing would put your privacy or safety at risk, consider praying the sentences or bringing them to a trusted support person.

Let yourself name what the event cost

The impact of a hurt can extend beyond the first moment. Consider what changed in your willingness to speak, how you entered a gathering, or what responsibilities became harder to carry. Put a name to one effect you can describe. A specific effect often gives you a more useful starting point for prayer.

Martha noticed that she had stopped responding to ordinary messages in the family chat. She still wanted to know about birthdays and gatherings. She wanted her financial details to stay private. These two facts helped her see that she could mute one conversation for a time while remaining connected to a relative she trusted.

Exercise. Complete the sentence “Since it happened, I have found it harder to ____.” Choose one effect to bring before God. Then write one thing you would like to protect in the coming week. Keep the two sentences somewhere appropriate to your circumstances.

practicingthanksgiving.excerpt:
Scripture reading · Psalm 103:1-14

Give memory something concrete to hold

Psalm 103 opens with David calling his own soul to bless the Lord and remember His benefits. The psalm moves through forgiveness, healing, redemption, steadfast love, and the Lord's compassion toward people whose frailty He knows. David remembers what God does and who God is. That breadth gives us language for thanksgiving beyond the things that happened to go our way.

Evelyn looked back over the previous week and first wrote, “Everything was difficult.” When she tried to remember Monday in detail, she could name the meal Mark brought. She also remembered that her sister had stayed on the phone while she sorted out a confusing schedule. Evelyn wrote both the weight of the week and the help she had received. The two statements let her remember the week more truthfully. Later, reading her notes, she could pray for her sister and thank God for the patience she had been shown.

Choose a short period you can recall, such as the last seven days. Look at a calendar or ask a family member to help you remember. Choose one mercy and describe what made it matter. You might remember forgiveness you received, a timely word, someone who stayed to listen, or the provision of daily needs. Try including the way the gift helped you respond to something else. A meal may have given you time to sit with someone. A patient conversation may have helped you speak more gently later.

Exercise. Write two lines beginning “This was hard” and “I am thankful for.” Add a date or a detail beside the second line. Read Psalm 103:8-14 and choose one description of the Lord that helps you give thanks. Return to this note at the end of the week and see what you remember more clearly.

Reflection. What mercy would you want another person in your household to remember about this week?

Remember mercy in the shape of the Psalm

Psalm 103 moves from the psalmist speaking to his own soul to a wider account of God's compassion and steadfast love. Read the opening verses with the later descriptions of the Lord in mind. Choose a word about God's character and let it guide what you remember and how you pray.

Evelyn read the Psalm after recalling a difficult week. The word compassion helped her remember that her sister had listened while she sorted out the schedule. She thanked God for that patience and considered how she could show the same kind of attention to her father that evening.

Exercise. Read Psalm 103:1-14 and choose one description of the Lord. Write one recent mercy that gives you a reason to thank Him. Then ask where you could carry the same kind of care into an ordinary responsibility.

Use a record to recover a forgotten detail

A calendar, note, or brief conversation can help you remember a mercy you missed. Choose a short period, look at what actually happened, and let the details correct a first impression. Give the hard events and the help each a place in the account.

Evelyn looked at Thursday on her calendar and remembered a call she had nearly forgotten. Her sister had stayed with her while she worked out a new plan. Evelyn added the time and what they had decided. The note helped her recognize the support and gave her a particular reason to thank her sister.

Exercise. Look at the last seven days and choose one moment you remember clearly. Write what was hard and what helped. Keep the two sentences beside one another and give thanks for the mercy you can name.

unx3y.excerpt:
So what ways can you stay calm, composed and maintain self-esteem in a difficult environment? Here are some key steps you may to consider as a launching pad to self-improvement.

Picture yourself as a Dart Board. Think of everything and everyone else around you as Dart Pins. As they strike, they damage your self-esteem and hurt you in so many ways. Now how can you stop them?

Dart Pin #1 : Work

Beware of “survival of the fittest theory that may occur in a negative work environment. Some places rather than encourage cooperation, turn into a war zone. It is easy to want to jump in, and start a non ending fight. Stop it! Stay out of this, it will hurt your self-esteem. See others in a work place as a way of learning. What can you glean from others’ experiences?

Dart Pin #2: Other People’s Behavior

You can’t change how other’s act, you can only change your response to how they act. You control yourself and not others. Don’t worry about the behaviors of others, worry about yours.

Dart Pin #3: Change

Change is painful. It forces us into an arena that is unfamiliar. It exposes our weaknesses. Gold is transformed by fire. It expands, but it ultimately ends up in the right shape that was intended. While change may cause you to hurt temporarily, if you look at it as an opportunity, you will discover new ways to self-improvement. For example you have a new job role, and much is expected. As you learn to ride the curtails of change, like a wave, it will surely carry you up.

Dart Pin #4: The Past

Cry if you must about the pain of the past, but don’t remain there. See it as a chance to learn, and a lesson point. If you stay too long at your pity party, it will eat you up!

Dart Pin #5: Perception

Two people can go through the same experience, but perception will determine their different outcomes. Do not get caught up in the negativities of the world. In every dark area, determine to find the light, even you have to be the light!

Dart Pin #6: Determination Theory

What determines who and what you are, is a mix of genetics and the environment. Remember that you do not have to follow the negative patterns that may be in your family. If your parent was an alcoholic, by changing or creating the right environment, you can determine that you do not fall into that same tunnel.

littleheartsoldtestament.excerpt:
Bible Basis / Genesis 1:1-2:3

Before there were trees, birds, or people, God made the heavens and the earth. God spoke, and there was light. He separated light from darkness, gathered the waters, and brought forth dry land. Plants grew, and God set lights in the sky to mark days and seasons.

God filled the waters with living creatures and the sky with birds. He made animals to live on the land. Then God made people in His image and gave them responsibility for the earth. God saw that everything He had made was very good. On the seventh day, God rested from His work.

KEY SCRIPTURE / GENESIS 1:1

In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.

WHAT WE LEARN

The world belongs to God. Every person has worth because God made people in His image.

TALK TOGETHER

What is one thing God made that you can care for today?

LET'S PRAY

Father, thank You for making the world and giving us a place in it. Help us care for what You made. Amen.

littleheartsnewtestament.excerpt:
Bible Basis: Luke 2:1-20

Caesar Augustus ordered a census, so Joseph traveled from Nazareth to Bethlehem, the town of David, with Mary, who was expecting Jesus. While they were there, the time came for the baby to be born.

Mary gave birth to her firstborn Son. She wrapped Him in cloths and laid Him in a manger because there was no suitable guest room available for them. Scripture does not tell us every detail of the place, but it tells us clearly that God's promised Savior entered the world in humility.

That same night, shepherds in the fields nearby received an announcement from an angel: a Savior had been born in David's town - Christ the Lord. After hearing the heavenly praise, the shepherds hurried to Bethlehem and found Mary, Joseph, and the baby lying in the manger. They told others what the angel had said, and everyone who heard their report wondered at it. Mary treasured these things in her heart. Jesus' birth shows that God keeps His promises and that salvation is His gift to the world.

Key Scripture

"She gave birth to her firstborn, a son... and placed him in a manger." — Luke 2:7

What We Learn

God keeps His promises. Jesus came into the world as our Savior, and His humble birth shows God's grace. Let's Pray

Father, thank You for sending Jesus our Savior. Help me receive Your love and remember that You always keep Your promises. Amen.

tRDg7.excerpt:
Synopsis

You really ought to let go of your picture of how you want it all to be. It means letting go of attempting to control things over which you've no control. Among the prime causes of our suffering is our wishing for matters to be different than they are. Yes, we all want a peaceful existence rather than a world filled with arms of mass destruction. Yes, we all wish for health rather than illness. Yes, we all wish for healthy, happy youngsters rather than youngsters who break our hearts. But occasionally life doesn't hand us what we wish. And when we let go of our needing it all to be a particular way, we may breathe a sigh of relief and open the door to a more potent way of living.

Faith To Relinquish

When you relinquish control in your life and relationships and have faith, you open a space in your life for something fresh to come in and let yourself release the stress. You're accepting what is and adjusting your energies and efforts towards other more positive actions. Cut down stress and anxiety by utilizing the following steps to relinquish control in your life.

There are so a lot of situations where you just wish to hang on to a particular way of believing, acting or doing things as you don't wish to be proven "wrong". Take a rich breath and relinquish the need to be correct. If you're attempting to control somebody else's behavior, realize that it isn't healthy for you or for that individual. Take a piece of paper and put down all your expectations of that individual and then rip up that sheet of paper and let them go. Quit fighting or resisting what is and alter your need to command the situation so that you are able to have some peace and recover that energy that you've been using up in an unfruitful place. Acknowledging that you're "incorrect" for hanging on in some instances may actually be very "right" for your life.

Occasionally just the cognizance that you're hanging on to control isn't enough. If you keep hanging on to control and use up unbelievable amounts of energy balking change, then sit down and work out precisely why. Take out your journal and put down the top 3 things that you'll let go of when you relinquish control. Do you fear that if you let go, you'll lose a relationship? Do you feel that if you alter your life-style, you'll lose your comfort zone? Are you nervous and stressed out at the thought of having change?

OzmMJ.excerpt:
Synopsis If you conceive of two hoi polloi praying for a mutual acquaintance to recover from an illness, you may be able to conceive of one of them thinking, "God, please save my acquaintance from his atrocious illness that my online research states kills thousands of individuals between the ages of in the prime of their life every year; please don't let this atrocious disease kill my acquaintance like it does so many others..." However may you conceive of the other friend merely envisioning himself having fun with his acquaintance – feeling thankful that the acquaintance was cured?

Think Of It This Way

Both of these individuals think they're praying for the acquaintance to recuperate; but the first friend is truly centering on the issue. They both wish the same thing; but only one of them was thinking of it.

It's too simple to think of the batch of bills instead of thinking of how thankful you feel having paid them off all in full. If you joke and think to yourself, "uh-huh, right; I would like to see the day all my notes were paid off..." then you're getting a first-hand look at the reality of your fundamental beliefs. You think in debt; and you will remain there as long as you do.

There are 2 fashions to pray for something:

By conceiving of the delight and gratitude that comes with the fresh matter; and, by bidding away the previous, or "foul," matter.

In addition to that, individuals utilize The Law of Attraction in much the same fashion: conceiving of, desiring, dreaming, wishing, and designing for the next fresh experience; or, wanting what they do not have, or wishing away what they do have.

Whether you name it prayer, or utilizing the Law of Attraction, centered thought will always bring about results; the content of your views brings forth the content of your consequences - and the nature of your ideas, favorable or damaging, determines the nature of your consequences.

tKgAC.excerpt:
Most followers of different religions tend to find some connection within the religion’s fundamentals and the morality issues, in a way that makes the two elements connect on some level of synchronicity. This would hopefully bring forth the ideal moral person who will be an asset to society and certainly a good individual to have as a partner in any relationship.

Find A Common Ground

In the interest of creating some level of harmony within a relationship where there are varied religious beliefs, both parties should be open and ready to evaluate the differences and similarities on both sides of the equation. Once this has been established clearly, they should then go about listing all the similarities found parallel to both religions so that some common ground can be clearly and successfully identified.

Through the process of identifying these similarities, both parties will be able to understand and work together in incorporating these beliefs into the daily lifestyle practices. This will not only help to create a strong understanding between each other, but will also help to give each other a sense of togetherness in practicing something they both have in common. Though most of these similarities should be practiced with some level of seriousness and respect, both parties will also be able to enjoy sharing such common ground, thus making it a more enjoyable experience overall. Acknowledging these similarities will also help to bring the parties closer together as they try to understand each other’s varied beliefs.

This evaluation process is also helpful if there are intentions to expand the current unit into a family unit. Bringing children into the picture is something that can be a point of contention when it comes to religious issues. Therefore, with the common ground previously established, this transition phase can be handled with care and respect.
